title: The Philidor defence
summary: Rook and pawn against rook: how to draw with the rook on the third rank and checks from behind.
part.third.title: The third rank
part.third.summary: King on the queening square, rook on the third rank and, once the pawn advances, checks from behind.
part.errors.title: Hasty mistakes
part.errors.summary: Checking too early, staying too long, and what to do when Black trades the rooks.
part.beyond.title: Other pawns and recap
part.beyond.summary: The same defence against a bishop's pawn, where it stops working, and the rules for your games.
step.intro: Rook and pawn against rook is the most common endgame in chess, and half the time you will be the one defending. This is the defence Philidor showed in 1777, and it solves most cases. It takes three things. Your king on the pawn's queening square. Your rook on the third rank, from end to end. And the black king still behind that line: as long as the rook is there, it cannot step onto the third rank, and without the king in front the pawn does not get through. Black has only one way to try something: advance the pawn.
step.take: First you have to get there. Your king is already on the queening square, but the rook is on the first rank. Bring it to the third and, as long as Black does not advance the pawn, keep strolling along it.
step.take.hint: Rb3. Then a waiting move on the same rank: Ra3.
step.take.done: The rank is yours. Notice that you do not need to do anything: it is Black who has to act.
step.pawn: Black has advanced the pawn to the third rank. Now everything changes. Your rook no longer holds anything there: the black king threatens to enter on f3 and mate with the rook on h1. But the advance has a price. The pawn has taken the square where the black king would hide from checks. So the rook goes to the far end of the board and checks from behind, and the black king has no shelter.
step.behind: Rook to the far end. When the black king threatens mate, start checking on its file and do not stop.
step.behind.hint: Ra8. After Kf3, Rf8+; and after each king move, check on the file where it stands.
step.behind.done: The black king has no shelter. If it walks away from the pawn, you attack the pawn with the rook; if it comes back, more checks. A draw. That is the whole defence: third rank until the pawn advances, then checks from behind.
step.early: Two mistakes spoil everything, and both come from haste. The first: checking too early. Here the rook left the third rank with the pawn still on the fourth. The black king entered on e3, the square the pawn has not taken yet, and it will not leave: the checks from behind run out, because the pawn covers it. And the black rook already threatens mate on a1 (Ra1#). Lost. The rook leaves the third rank only after the pawn steps onto it.
step.passive: The second mistake is the opposite: staying. The pawn has advanced and the rook remained on the third rank. The black king entered on f3 and threatens mate on h1. Taking the pawn with check does not help: the king recaptures. Lost as well. On the very move the pawn steps onto the third rank, the rook goes to the far end, not one move later.
step.trade: One last resource for Black: blocking the checks with the rook and forcing the exchange. Do not be afraid. The king and pawn ending that remains is a draw, on one condition: your king retreats straight back, in front of the pawn.
step.endgame: Give the check, exchange rooks and hold the pawn ending. At the end the king returns to the queening square.
step.endgame.hint: Rd8+, Rxd5+, Ke2 and, when the black king comes close, Ke1.
step.endgame.done: With the king on e1, in front of the pawn, the black king cannot drive it out: if the pawn advances with check, you step back in front of it and it is stalemate. Retreating sideways, to d1 or f1, would lose.
step.bishop: The defence works against any pawn. Here it is a bishop's pawn and the pieces are scattered, but the recipe is the same: the rook takes the third rank. In this case it is almost the only move, because Black threatens to walk in with the king.
step.limits: And when the defence is not ready? Here the black king is already beside the pawn and your rook is stuck on the fourth rank: dropping to the third loses. It is still a draw, but by another road: the rook goes to the far end of the file and then behind the pawn, and the king runs to the short side. That is next lesson's defence. Just remember this: Philidor is the easy draw; when it slips away there is still a defence, but it demands precision.
step.recap: Three rules. One: king on the queening square and rook on the third rank, waiting. Two: when the pawn steps onto the third rank, the rook goes to the far end and checks from behind; not before, not after. Three: if the rooks come off, the king retreats straight back, in front of the pawn.
step.t_classic: This is the Philidor position, and you defend with White. Before I explain: what stops the black king from advancing, and what can Black still try?
step.t_classic.hint1: Look at the rank your rook is on. Which squares does it deny the black king?
step.t_bishop: Now a bishop's pawn, with the pieces scattered. Black threatens to bring the king in. Which move sets up the defence?
step.t_bishop.hint1: The recipe does not depend on the pawn: find the rank the black king cannot cross.
step.finish: Now against the machine, from the start: take the third rank, wait for the pawn to advance and give the checks from behind.
ex.e01: White to move and draw. The king is already on the queening square. Where does the rook need to be?
ex.e01.hint: On the rank that stops the black king from advancing.
ex.e01.solution: Rb3. The rook takes the third rank and the black king does not get through. Running the rook up the b-file to the far end also draws, but it is harder work: the third rank is the simple way.
ex.e02: White to move and draw. The pawn has just advanced to the third rank. What now?
ex.e02.hint: The third rank no longer protects anything. The black king has lost its shelter.
ex.e02.solution: Ra8 (or a7, a6, a5): the rook goes far away, to check from behind. Staying on the third rank loses: the black king enters on f3 with a mating threat.
ex.e03: White to move and draw. The black king entered on f3 and threatens mate on h1. Only one move saves the game.
ex.e03.solution: Rf8+. The black king has to step aside, and the checks go on: it has nowhere to hide, because the pawn occupies the shelter square.
ex.e04: White to move and draw. A bishop's pawn, and Black threatens to advance the king. Set up the defence.
ex.e04.solution: Rg3. With the rook on the third rank the black king cannot enter on d3 or c3. The king move to c1 also draws, but this is the Philidor defence.
ex.e05: White to move and draw. The rooks have been exchanged. Where does the king go?
ex.e05.hint: Straight back, in front of the pawn.
ex.e05.solution: Ke1. If the black king goes to d3, you stand opposite it on d1; if the pawn advances with check, the king returns to e1 and the black king either lets go of the pawn or stalemates. Kd1 and Kf1 lose: the black king takes the opposition.
ex.e06: White to move and draw. The Philidor position, with you to move. Play the whole defence: wait, and react when the pawn advances.
ex.e06.hint: A waiting move on the third rank. When the pawn advances, rook to the far end; when the king threatens mate, check.
ex.e06.solution: Rb3, waiting. After e3, Rb8; and after Kf3, Rf8+. Third rank until the pawn advances, then checks from behind.
ex.e07: White to move and draw. In the middle of the checks the black king came to d3 and its rook threatens mate. What is the move?
ex.e07.solution: Rd8+. Any quiet move would allow mate on h1. With check after check the black king has to walk away from the pawn, and then the rook attacks it.
ex.e08: White to move and draw. Black wants to block the check with the rook. Exchange and hold the pawn ending.
ex.e08.hint: Check, exchange, and the king goes in front of the pawn. The last king move is the one that matters.
ex.e08.solution: Rd8+, Rxd5+, Ke2 and, after Kd4, Ke1. The king retreats straight to the queening square, and the pawn ending is a draw.
ex.e09: White to move and draw. The black rook is checking to drive your king off the queening square. Return to it and complete the defence.
ex.e09.hint: The king steps out of check and returns to e1. When the pawn advances, you know what to do.
ex.e09.solution: Ke2, Ke1 and, after e3, Ra8 and Rf8+. The black rook's checks change nothing: the king returns to the queening square and the rook stays on the third rank until the pawn advances.
ex.e10: White to move and draw. The third rank no longer works: dropping the rook there loses. Find the other road.
ex.e10.hint: The rook goes to the far end of the file and, next move, behind the pawn.
ex.e10.solution: Rf7 (or another square at the far end of the f-file) and, after Kd3, Re7: the rook behind the pawn stops it advancing. To the check on h1 the king goes to f2. It is next lesson's defence.
key.classic: The Philidor position (1777), as shown on Wikipedia, with colours reversed: king on the queening square and rook on the third rank. A draw whoever is to move.
key.reach: The third rank still has to be taken: Rb3. It is the "Philidor Position" chapter of the Lichess practice, with colours reversed.
key.bishop: With a bishop's pawn the defence is the same: Rg3. From Yuri61's Lichess study, with colours reversed.
key.advanced: The third rank no longer works: rook to the far end and then behind the pawn. The "Advanced Philidor" chapter of the Lichess practice, with colours reversed.
history: François-André Philidor published this defence in 1777, in the second edition of his Analysis of the Game of Chess, and believed it was the only way to draw this endgame. For more than a century the manuals repeated his analysis, including a variation in which he gave the game up as lost if the rook left the third rank early. In 1897 Max Karstedt showed that there were other defences, and today the tablebases confirm it: in that variation of Philidor's the position was still a draw. The third-rank defence, however, remains the simplest of all, and it is the first one every player should know by heart.
practice: Now against the machine: you have only the rook, it has the rook and the pawn. Take the third rank, wait for the pawn to advance and check from behind. The goal is to draw.
